title: Informal understanding of system expectations
description: Teams have a rough, undocumented view of what “good enough” performance and quality looks like for their systems. Expectations vary by individual and are rarely written down. There is little link between system behaviour and business outcomes.

title: Basic non functional expectations captured
description: Key systems have simple, documented expectations for response time, error rates and data quality. These are usually captured in design docs or tickets but not consistently reviewed. Business stakeholders are aware of the expectations but do not actively manage to them.

title: Defined quality attributes for key services
description: Important services have agreed quality attributes such as performance, reliability and data accuracy tied to user journeys. These attributes are documented, reviewed at least annually and used to guide design and acceptance criteria. Trade offs are explicit and risk based.

title: Outcome driven design standards
description: Design standards require engineers to consider performance, quality and resilience up front for new or changed services. Architectural reviews check evidence that quality attributes are addressed using patterns that have worked in production. Business and technology collaborate to balance speed and quality based on risk.

title: Continuous evolution of quality expectations
description: Quality attributes and service expectations are regularly refined using real operational and user experience data. Scenario analysis and experiments are used to validate whether designs will hold up under new business models, channels or regulations. The organisation can show how design decisions today anticipate future resilience needs.

title: Manual testing by individuals
description: Testing is mostly manual and informal, done by developers or a small test team before releases. Coverage is patchy and relies heavily on individual knowledge. Regression issues are common after changes.

title: Basic scripted and acceptance testing
description: Key user flows have simple test scripts or checklists that are followed during changes. Unit tests exist for some components, often driven by individual developers. Testing is repeatable but still largely manual and not risk based.

title: Automated regression and integration testing
description: Automated tests cover core business logic, key integrations and common failure paths. Tests run as part of the build or deployment pipeline and must pass before promotion to production. Coverage and failed tests are tracked, with defects feeding a visible backlog.

title: Risk based and performance aware testing
description: Testing strategy is tailored by risk, with higher risk services getting deeper functional, performance and negative path testing. Load and performance tests are integrated into pipelines for critical systems. Test results are monitored over time to identify trends and weak spots.

title: Continuous validation in and before production
description: The organisation uses techniques like feature flags, canary releases and synthetic monitoring to continuously validate behaviour with real traffic. Test suites are regularly updated based on incident learnings and new failure modes. Teams can demonstrate that quality checks evolve as the system and threat landscape change.

title: Local logs and basic health checks
description: Individual teams enable local logs and simple health checks, but coverage varies widely. There is no standard for what is logged and it is hard to get a system wide view of performance or errors. Troubleshooting relies on logging into servers or reading application logs manually.

title: Central logs for critical systems
description: Critical applications send logs to a central platform, usually for security or audit reasons. Some dashboards or searches exist, but they are not consistently maintained. Performance metrics are monitored for a few key components, often infrastructure rather than end user experience.

title: Standardised observability for key services
description: Key services emit standard logs, metrics and alerts that allow teams to see request rates, latency, errors and saturation. Dashboards exist for core user journeys, with alerts for defined thresholds. Teams use these views during incidents and regular service reviews.

title: End to end performance and user experience monitoring
description: The organisation can trace performance from end user to back end, including APIs and data platforms. Synthetic tests and real user monitoring are in place for critical journeys. Performance regressions after changes are detected quickly and linked back to specific deployments or configuration changes.

title: Data driven optimisation of performance and quality
description: Product and engineering teams use observability data to continuously optimise performance and quality in line with business priorities. They experiment, set improvement targets and measure impact on users and operations. Cross system metrics help identify systemic issues, not just local ones.

title: Defects tracked inconsistently
description: Defects are recorded in ad hoc ways or kept in personal lists. Severity and impact are not consistently assessed. Technical debt is rarely captured except in developer notes.

title: Basic defect backlog for key systems
description: Defects for important systems are logged in a shared tool with severity and priority fields. There is some effort to group and triage issues, but backlogs can become cluttered or stale. Technical debt items are captured sporadically.

title: Managed backlog and debt register
description: Defects and technical debt are recorded in a structured backlog with clear owners, priorities and target fix windows. Risk and customer impact are considered during triage. Teams review their backlog regularly and can show what they plan to fix versus accept as known risk.

title: Risk based remediation and trend tracking
description: The organisation tracks trends in defects, incidents and customer complaints and uses this to focus remediation. Technical debt is logged with clear risk descriptions and is included in planning and funding conversations. High risk items have time bound remediation plans that are actively monitored.

title: Systemic quality and debt management
description: Defect and debt data is used to identify systemic issues in architecture, tooling or ways of working. Senior leaders review quality risk alongside other business risks. The organisation can evidence the impact of sustained investment in quality and show that the overall risk profile is improving.

title: Uncontrolled releases and hotfixes
description: Releases are done manually with little documentation or approval. Hotfixes are common and often made directly in production. There is limited traceability of what changed and when.

title: Basic release checklist and approvals
description: Releases follow a simple checklist and require sign off from a product or technical lead. Some changes are grouped into release windows. Rollback is possible but not often rehearsed.

title: Standardised build and deployment process
description: Most services use a defined build and deployment process with version control, peer review and promotion through environments. Releases are logged, with clear links to change tickets and test evidence. Rollback procedures are documented and known.

title: Automated, low risk deployments
description: Automated pipelines perform builds, tests and deployments for key services. Smaller, more frequent releases reduce change risk. Techniques like blue green or canary deployments are used for higher risk systems. Change success rates and change related incidents are tracked.

title: Continuous delivery with built in safety
description: Teams can deploy when needed without central release gates, using guardrails and automated checks. Business and technology jointly decide where to increase or decrease release frequency based on risk and value. The deployment process is regularly improved using incident and performance data.

title: No formal service level objectives
description: Availability is discussed informally in terms like “always on” without clear targets. Outages are judged case by case. There is no shared definition of what counts as downtime for key services.

title: Uptime targets for some services
description: Some critical services have simple uptime targets or SLAs, usually defined in contracts or internal documents. Measurement is approximate and often based on incident records rather than continuous monitoring.

title: Defined and monitored SLOs for key services
description: For important services, service level objectives and error budgets are agreed and measured using monitoring data. SLOs are defined in terms of user experience where possible. Breaches trigger review and discussions about prioritising reliability work.

title: Reliability managed as a product concern
description: Product and engineering teams treat reliability as a feature, planning work to maintain SLOs based on error budget consumption. Trade offs between new features and reliability are explicit. SLOs are reviewed regularly as usage patterns and business priorities change.

title: Adaptive, ecosystem aware reliability goals
description: SLOs account for dependencies on third party services, networks and data providers. Scenario analysis is used to set realistic but stretching reliability goals. The organisation can explain how its reliability posture supports wider ecosystem resilience, such as critical national infrastructure or partner supply chains.

title: Single instance and single region designs
description: Many systems rely on a single instance, data store or site. Failures of a single component can lead to full service outages. Resilience is mostly based on hardware reliability and manual interventions.

title: Basic redundancy for critical components
description: Some critical components have redundancy, such as simple clustering or replication. Failover is possible but may be manual or untested. Dependencies and single points of failure are not systematically documented.

title: Resilience patterns used for key services
description: Important services use resilience patterns such as multi availability zone deployments, connection pooling and retry logic. Dependencies are mapped and obvious single points of failure are addressed. Architectural standards mention resilience expectations for new services.

title: Designed for graceful degradation and failover
description: Services are designed to degrade gracefully under failure or overload, for example by limiting non essential features. Multi region or multi provider strategies are used where justified. Failover mechanisms are tested regularly and measured for time to recover.

title: Systemic reliability engineering
description: Resilience engineering practices such as chaos testing and failure analysis are used to understand how systems behave under stress. Architectural decisions consider systemic risks like common mode failures, shared control planes and complex dependency chains. The organisation can show how resilience patterns have reduced the impact of real incidents.

title: Ad hoc incident handling
description: When an outage occurs, people scramble informally to fix it. There is no clear incident owner, communication plan or consistent logging of what happened. Learnings are often lost.

title: Basic incident process for major outages
description: Major incidents follow a simple process with an incident manager and communication to stakeholders. Some incidents are recorded in a shared tool. On call arrangements exist but are not always clear or documented for all services.

title: Structured incident management and on call
description: There is a defined incident management process with severity levels, roles and communication templates. On call rotas and escalation paths are documented and tested. Post incident reviews happen for significant outages, with actions tracked to completion.

title: Integrated incident command and observability
description: Incident responders have access to shared dashboards, logs and runbooks to diagnose issues quickly. Incidents are correlated across systems and channels. Business stakeholders receive timely, accurate updates and can help prioritise recovery steps.

title: Continuous improvement from availability incidents
description: Incident data is analysed to identify systemic issues and improvement themes. The organisation runs game days and simulations to rehearse response to complex failures. On call and incident work is recognised, measured and managed to avoid burnout.

title: Ad hoc backups, rarely tested
description: Some backups exist but are not consistently configured or documented. Recovery time and data loss in a severe incident are largely unknown. Restores are rare and often fail when needed.

title: Basic backup policy for key data
description: Critical databases and file stores are backed up on a schedule. Retention periods are defined in a simple policy. Periodic test restores are carried out, but not always documented or aligned to business recovery needs.

title: Defined recovery objectives and tested restores
description: Recovery time and recovery point objectives are agreed for key services. Backup and restore procedures are documented and tested at least annually. Results of tests are recorded, with remediation actions assigned where gaps are found.

title: Integrated continuity and recovery planning
description: Business continuity, disaster recovery and IT recovery plans are aligned and exercised together. Secondary sites, regions or alternative channels are available for critical services. The organisation can demonstrate that recovery capabilities keep pace with changes in architecture and data volumes.

title: Adaptive continuity and recovery capabilities
description: Recovery plans are regularly updated based on scenarios, incidents and changes in the external environment. Dependencies on third parties and shared services are understood and included in exercises. The organisation participates in sector or ecosystem level resilience exercises where relevant.

title: Changes made directly in production
description: Some system changes, including configuration and database updates, are made directly in production. There is little formal assessment of availability risk before deployment. Outages caused by changes are common.

title: Basic change approvals for high risk work
description: A change advisory process exists for higher risk changes, often focusing on infrastructure. Assessment of availability impact is largely subjective. Rollback plans are requested but not always detailed.

title: Standard change types and deployment windows
description: Common low risk changes follow a streamlined process, while higher risk changes get more scrutiny. Deployment windows are chosen to reduce customer impact. Change success and failure rates are monitored.

title: Engineering led change risk mitigation
description: Engineering teams use techniques like staging, configuration as code and automated tests to reduce change risk. Change risk assessments explicitly reference SLOs, dependencies and blast radius. Rollback and mitigation steps are rehearsed for critical changes.

title: Dynamic, data informed change control
description: Change policies adapt based on real world risk and performance. For example, services with a good change history and strong guardrails get faster paths, while fragile systems receive additional controls. The organisation can show how change governance supports both reliability and delivery speed.

title: Implicit security responsibilities
description: Security is seen as an IT or compliance issue handled by a small team. Roles and responsibilities are not clearly documented. Decisions are often reactive to audit findings or incidents.

title: Basic policies and senior sponsorship
description: Core security policies exist and are approved by senior leadership. A nominated security leader or CISO role is in place, even if part time. Policies are communicated, but enforcement and measurement are limited.

title: Risk based security governance
description: Security governance is built around a risk register, with regular reviews and clear ownership of key risks. Policies link to practical controls and are aligned with legal and regulatory requirements. Security is represented in key change and design forums.

title: Integrated security and business decision making
description: Security risk is considered alongside financial, operational and reputational risk in decision forums. Business units understand their role in managing security. Exceptions to policy are tracked, time bound and justified by risk.

title: Systemic, ecosystem aware security governance
description: Governance recognises dependencies on partners, suppliers and shared platforms. The organisation contributes to sector or national security initiatives where relevant. Scenario exercises and threat intelligence inform strategic risk decisions, not just control checklists.

title: Shared accounts and weak authentication
description: Shared admin accounts and local credentials are common. Password policies are basic or inconsistently applied. Multi factor authentication is rare.

title: Central directory for core systems
description: A central identity store exists for employees and is used by key applications. Basic role based access is in place. Multi factor authentication is enabled for some higher risk access, such as remote admin.

title: Standardised identity and access lifecycle
description: Joiner, mover and leaver processes are defined and integrated with HR events. Most systems use central identity and single sign on. Privileged access is restricted, logged and reviewed regularly.

title: Strong, adaptive access controls
description: Multi factor authentication is the norm for privileged and remote access. Access reviews are risk based and automated where possible. Conditional access and just in time elevation are used for sensitive operations.

title: Identity as a security and resilience control plane
description: Identity is used as a consistent control plane across on premises, cloud and SaaS. The organisation monitors and tunes identity signals to detect abuse and unusual patterns. Plans exist to maintain access control in the face of identity provider outages or compromises.

title: Local logs with limited review
description: Systems generate logs, but they are stored locally or in separate tools. Security relevant events are rarely reviewed unless after an incident. There is no central view of suspicious activity.

title: Central logging for key systems
description: Logs from critical infrastructure and applications are collected centrally. A few basic correlation rules and dashboards exist. Analysts mainly search manually during investigations.

title: Defined detection use cases and alerting
description: The organisation maintains a set of high value detection use cases such as privileged misuse, unusual data access and policy violations. Alerts are tuned to reduce noise and routed to an operations or security team. Playbooks exist for common alerts.

title: Threat informed and behaviour based detection
description: Detections are informed by current threat intelligence and real incidents. Behaviour and anomaly based techniques complement rule based alerts. Coverage is regularly assessed against reference models or frameworks.

title: Continuous improvement of detection coverage
description: Detection quality is measured through tests, simulations and purple team exercises. Gaps are fed into a roadmap and addressed in a structured way. Detection content and telemetry are adjusted as the environment and threat landscape evolve.

title: Ad hoc security incident handling
description: Security incidents are handled as general IT issues. There is no specific playbook, classification scheme or crisis escalation path. External reporting obligations may be missed.

title: Basic security incident response plan
description: A documented incident response plan exists, covering roles, high level steps and regulatory reporting triggers. The security team coordinates most security incidents, but not all staff know how to contact them quickly.

title: Structured security incident management
description: Incidents are classified by type and severity, with clear workflows. Evidence handling, containment, eradication and recovery steps are defined. After action reviews are held for serious incidents, with actions tracked.

title: Crisis management and stakeholder engagement
description: Security incidents that could affect customers, regulators or the public are handled through an integrated crisis management process. Communication plans and decision thresholds are rehearsed. The organisation maintains relationships with external partners such as law enforcement or national bodies where appropriate.

title: Proactive preparation and exercising
description: Regular tabletop and technical exercises test response to realistic attack scenarios, including supply chain incidents and data extortion. Lessons learned influence controls, architecture and contracts. The organisation can demonstrate improved response times and reduced impact over time.

title: Security considered late in development
description: Security issues tend to surface during testing or after go live. Developers rely on general awareness rather than specific secure coding standards. Configuration is often managed manually.

title: Basic secure coding guidance and reviews
description: Secure coding guidelines exist and are shared with developers. Code reviews touch on security, for example avoiding obvious injection or hard coded secrets. Some static analysis tools may be used, but findings are not always triaged.

title: Integrated security testing in pipelines
description: Static and dynamic security tests are integrated into build or deployment pipelines for key applications. Libraries and dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities. Security findings are triaged and tracked to closure.

title: Secure by design and configuration as code
description: Security requirements are captured during design, including data classification and access controls. Infrastructure and configuration are managed as code, reviewed and tested. Threat modeling is performed for higher risk systems.

title: Continuous, collaborative secure engineering
description: Security engineers and developers work together throughout the lifecycle. Patterns and reusable components simplify secure implementation. The organisation measures and improves the time from vulnerability discovery to remediation across its estate.

title: Limited view of sensitive data
description: Sensitive data is known in some systems but there is no complete map. Classification is ad hoc and labels are inconsistent. Controls vary by application.

title: Basic data classification and handling rules
description: Data is classified into a small number of categories with associated handling rules. Some systems enforce encryption at rest and in transit. Staff receive awareness training on handling sensitive data.

title: Consistent protection across key data stores
description: Sensitive data locations are documented for core systems. Encryption, access control and logging are consistently applied for these stores. Data retention and disposal rules are implemented for some data sets.

title: Lifecycle management and privacy by design
description: Data lifecycle is considered during design, including minimisation, retention and deletion. Privacy impact assessments are performed where required. Data protection controls are tested and monitored.

title: Adaptive data protection and ethics
description: Data protection measures adapt to emerging threats and regulatory changes. The organisation considers ethical use of data, not just legal compliance. Cross functional teams review high risk data uses and can show how harm to individuals and society is mitigated.

title: Limited view of supplier security risk
description: Supplier selection focuses on price and functionality. Security is mentioned in contracts but not examined in depth. There is little understanding of how third parties affect overall resilience.

title: Basic security clauses in contracts
description: Standard security and confidentiality clauses appear in most new contracts. Higher risk suppliers may be asked to complete a questionnaire. Ongoing assurance is rare and often manual.

title: Tiered supplier risk management
description: Suppliers are categorised by criticality and data sensitivity. Due diligence requirements and monitoring are defined per tier. Some suppliers provide independent assurance reports or certifications.

title: Integrated third party resilience oversight
description: The organisation tracks dependencies on cloud, SaaS and outsourced providers and understands the impact of their failure. Contracts include resilience, incident notification and testing expectations. Supplier incidents are included in internal reporting.

title: Collaborative supply chain security
description: The organisation collaborates with key suppliers and peers on threat information, incident exercises and improvement programs. It evaluates concentration risk and plans for alternative suppliers or failover where appropriate. Supply chain resilience is part of strategic planning.

title: Change awareness driven by individuals
description: Awareness of new threats, technologies or regulations depends on individual interest. There is no structured way to share or act on this information. Responses are reactive when change hits.

title: Basic horizon scanning in some teams
description: Some teams follow industry news, vendor briefings or government alerts. Insights are occasionally shared in meetings or emails. There is no systematic link to risk or strategy.

title: Structured horizon scanning and risk input
description: A regular process exists to review external developments such as threat reports, regulations and technology trends. Outcomes feed into risk registers, roadmaps and training plans. Responsibilities for scanning are defined.

title: Cross functional foresight and scenario thinking
description: Business, technology and risk functions jointly consider how changes could affect services and customers. Scenario workshops explore plausible futures. Output informs investment and architecture choices.

title: Continuous sensing and strategic adaptation
description: The organisation has feedback loops from incidents, customers, regulators and partners that inform strategy. It can give examples where early sensing of change led to proactive moves that improved resilience or created advantage.

title: Experiments are rare and informal
description: Trying new tools or ways of working is difficult due to process or risk concerns. Experiments happen in isolated pockets and are not shared. Failure is often discouraged.

title: Small pilots with limited structure
description: Teams sometimes run pilots or proofs of concept, usually with vendor support. These are documented in basic terms. Success criteria and learning capture are inconsistent.

title: Defined approach to safe experimentation
description: There is a clear way to run safe to try experiments, including guardrails for data, security and customer impact. Experiments have hypotheses and success measures. Outcomes are shared beyond the immediate team.

title: Portfolio of resilience oriented experiments
description: A portion of capacity is reserved for experiments that could improve resilience, such as new observability, automation or architecture patterns. Results influence standards and roadmaps. Leadership supports learning from experiments that did not deliver expected benefits.

title: Experimentation embedded in ways of working
description: Continuous experimentation is part of product and platform teams’ normal work. The organisation can show a track record of scaling experiments into production improvements and retiring unhelpful approaches quickly.

title: Lessons rarely captured from incidents
description: After incidents or near misses, fixes are applied but formal learning is minimal. The same types of issues recur. Knowledge remains in individuals’ heads.

title: Basic post incident reviews
description: Some incidents have a short review meeting or document. Actions are identified but may not be tracked systematically. Focus is often on blame rather than system learning.

title: Structured, blameless learning practices
description: Post incident reviews use a standard template focused on contributing factors and system behaviour. Actions are recorded, owned and tracked. Near misses and success stories are also discussed where time allows.

title: Shared learning across teams and domains
description: Insights from reviews are shared across teams and domains, for example via brown bag sessions or internal reports. Patterns and themes are identified and addressed in roadmaps, training or policy updates.

title: Continuous learning culture
description: Learning from incidents, changes and experiments is highly valued and visible in leadership behaviour. The organisation can show how lessons have led to changes in systems, contracts and structures that reduced risk over time.

title: No regular scenario exercises
description: The organisation relies on real incidents to test its resilience. Staff have limited practice responding to complex or cross team events.

title: Occasional tabletop exercises
description: Some tabletop exercises are run for compliance or training, often focused on a single scenario like ransomware. Feedback is captured but follow up may be limited.

title: Planned scenario and stress testing program
description: There is a schedule of scenario exercises covering different impact types such as cyber, cloud outage and data breach. Exercises involve relevant functions and suppliers where possible. Actions and gaps are documented and tracked.

title: Realistic, cross ecosystem exercising
description: Scenarios are designed around realistic, multi party events such as sector wide disruptions or simultaneous failures. Technical and business responders participate together. Exercise findings influence strategy, architecture and contracts.

title: Continuous scenario refinement and innovation
description: Scenario design evolves based on emerging risks, threat intelligence and lessons from real incidents. The organisation helps shape industry or national level exercising where relevant. Progress can be evidenced through improved response metrics and reduced surprises.

title: Siloed teams and limited collaboration
description: Teams work within narrow boundaries. Cross functional collaboration on resilience topics is rare. Psychological safety is low, so people may hide issues.

title: Some cross team initiatives
description: There are occasional cross functional projects or working groups, often driven by specific incidents or audits. Training on resilience topics is available but not widespread.

title: Established cross functional forums
description: Regular forums bring together product, operations, security and risk to discuss resilience topics. Training plans address key skills such as incident command, observability and secure design. Staff feel more comfortable raising concerns.

title: Resilience minded culture and leadership
description: Leaders talk about and reward behaviours that support resilience, such as early risk raising and collaborative problem solving. Stories of good practice are shared. Cross functional communities of practice exist for key themes.

title: Adaptive, learning oriented organisation
description: The organisation is comfortable adapting roles, processes and structures when needed. People at different levels can describe how their work contributes to resilience. Collaboration extends beyond the organisation to partners, customers and regulators.

title: Inconsistent logging of key actions
description: Some systems log important events, but there is no standard. Logs are often overwritten or hard to access. It can be difficult to reconstruct who did what and when.

title: Central log storage for important systems
description: Logs from key infrastructure and applications are retained in central storage for a defined period. Access is controlled. However, log quality and coverage vary and are not routinely reviewed.

title: Standardised audit logging for critical activities
description: Critical actions such as access changes, configuration updates and data exports are consistently logged with sufficient detail. Log schemas and retention are defined. Teams can demonstrate how they would retrieve evidence for a given time period or user.

title: Evidence capture integrated into processes
description: Systems and workflows are designed to capture evidence automatically for approvals, exceptions and key business decisions. Logs and records are linked to tickets or cases. Auditors and investigators can self serve common evidence sets.

title: Proactive evidence readiness
description: Evidence needs for regulators, customers and internal assurance are anticipated and designed in. The organisation tests its ability to produce evidence under time pressure. Logging and record keeping adapt when new systems or regulations are introduced.

title: Limited end to end traceability
description: It is hard to trace a transaction or data item across systems. Investigations rely on manual correlation and staff knowledge. Data lineage is mostly undocumented.

title: Basic tracing for some processes
description: For some key processes there are diagrams or documents showing which systems are involved. Logs may include shared identifiers that can be used to piece together a path.

title: Defined traceability for critical journeys
description: Critical customer and regulatory journeys have defined identifiers that follow them through systems. Tools or standard queries exist to reconstruct these journeys from logs and databases. Data lineage is documented for key data sets.

title: Tool supported tracing and investigations
description: Observability, logging and case management tools provide near real time tracing for important flows. Investigations use standard playbooks and repeatable queries. Findings are reproducible and can be shared with external parties if needed.

title: System wide traceability as a design principle
description: New services are required to support traceability and lineage standards. The organisation can show accurate end to end views of complex processes across internal and external systems. Traceability supports both resilience investigations and business optimisation.

title: Incomplete asset and configuration records
description: Hardware, software and cloud assets are recorded in multiple, inconsistent lists. Some critical systems may not be fully documented. Configuration changes are not tracked centrally.

title: Basic asset inventory for key environments
description: An inventory exists for critical servers, networks and cloud accounts. Ownership is recorded, but accuracy and completeness are not regularly verified. Configuration data is captured in some tools.

title: Managed asset and configuration baseline
description: The organisation maintains a reasonably complete inventory of assets, including cloud resources and key SaaS services. Configuration baselines exist for important platforms. Changes are tracked and can be reported over time.

title: Integrated asset, config and data flow view
description: Asset and configuration data is linked to services, data flows and owners. It is possible to answer questions like “where is this data processed” or “which systems depend on this component” using available records. Accuracy is checked regularly.

title: Dynamic, accurate view of the estate
description: Discovery, CMDB and configuration as code practices keep asset and configuration information up to date. Data lineage and system dependencies are visible for both on premises and cloud. This information is used during incidents, change planning and risk assessments.

title: Compliance activities driven by audits
description: Compliance requirements are addressed when audits or regulatory reviews arise. Evidence collection is manual and stressful. Control ownership is unclear.

title: Defined control library and owners
description: A basic library of controls exists for main regulations or frameworks. Control owners are named and understand their responsibilities. Evidence is stored in shared locations but may be fragmented.

title: Planned assurance and control testing
description: There is an annual or multi year assurance plan. Key controls are tested on a schedule, with results recorded and issues tracked. Gaps and exceptions are logged with remediation plans.

title: Continuous control monitoring where feasible
description: For some controls, automated monitoring replaces or supplements periodic testing. Dashboards show control status and exceptions. Assurance activities are coordinated across security, risk and internal audit.

title: Integrated, risk based assurance
description: Assurance focuses on areas of highest risk, informed by incidents, change and external developments. The organisation can demonstrate alignment between controls, risks and business objectives. Regulatory relationships are proactive rather than purely reactive.

title: Reactive response to capacity issues
description: Capacity problems are typically discovered when systems slow down or fail. Responses are manual, such as adding servers or asking users to retry later. Capacity planning is ad hoc.

title: Basic capacity thresholds for key components
description: Some monitoring exists for CPU, memory and storage thresholds on critical systems. When alerts fire, teams adjust capacity. Forward planning is based on rough estimates or past incidents.

title: Data informed capacity planning for key services
description: Usage data and growth trends are used to forecast capacity needs for important services. Plans consider peak loads, seasonal patterns and business events. Capacity risks are documented and discussed with stakeholders.

title: Integrated capacity planning across platforms
description: Capacity plans account for dependencies across infrastructure, applications and data platforms. Cloud and on premises resources are considered together. Capacity is aligned with SLOs and cost constraints.

title: Adaptive capacity strategy
description: Capacity plans are regularly updated based on real usage and experiments. The organisation can demonstrate how it prepares for new products, channels or regulations that may significantly change load. Capacity risk is part of enterprise risk discussions.

title: Mostly static infrastructure
description: Systems are provisioned for peak load manually. Scaling up or down is slow and requires significant effort. Overprovisioning or underprovisioning is common.

title: Basic horizontal scaling for some components
description: Some web or stateless tiers can be scaled horizontally, often with manual steps. Cloud auto scaling may be enabled but not tuned. Stateful components remain static.

title: Managed elasticity for key services
description: Critical services make use of auto scaling, queueing or other elasticity mechanisms. Scaling policies are defined and monitored. Capacity changes are logged and reviewed.

title: Elasticity patterns standardised and reused
description: Architectural patterns promote elastic design for new services, such as stateless compute, managed data stores and decoupled components. Platform teams provide reusable services and guidance. Elasticity is considered in change and design reviews.

title: Elasticity aligned with resilience and cost
description: Elasticity strategies are designed to support both resilience and efficient spend. The organisation can show how scaling behaviour during real events protected services while controlling cost. Elasticity patterns evolve as platforms and business needs change.

title: Little control over system demand
description: All requests are treated equally. During overload, systems fail in unpredictable ways. There is limited ability to protect critical workloads.

title: Basic rate limits for some interfaces
description: Some APIs or services have simple rate limits to prevent abuse. Limit values are not always tuned and may frustrate users. Manual actions are needed to adjust limits during events.

title: Demand management for critical paths
description: Critical services implement throttling, queuing or prioritisation for high value transactions. Graceful error messages or alternative channels exist for lower priority requests during overload. Decisions on who is protected are documented.

title: Coordinated demand shaping across systems
description: Demand management is considered across related systems, not just individual components. For example, bots, batch jobs or non urgent reporting can be slowed or paused during peak periods. Operators have playbooks to adjust demand controls during incidents.

title: Dynamic demand control based on risk and value
description: Demand controls adapt in near real time based on metrics and business priorities. The organisation can explain how it would protect critical users or services during extreme events, using data from past incidents and simulations.

title: Load testing rarely performed
description: Systems are assumed to cope without explicit testing. Load tests, if any, are run only before major go lives. Results are not reused.

title: One off load tests for critical launches
description: For some important projects, a load test is performed and basic issues are fixed. Tests focus on expected traffic levels and are not repeated later.

title: Regular load testing for key services
description: Key services have periodic load or stress tests, for example annually or before major events. Results are documented, with clear understanding of failure points and safety margins. Tests are designed with input from business and operations.

title: Integrated load and resilience testing
description: Load tests also check resilience features such as failover, throttling and graceful degradation. Automated or scripted load tests are part of pre production verification for critical changes. Findings feed into capacity, architecture and incident plans.

title: Continuous performance and stress experimentation
description: The organisation runs smaller, more frequent experiments to validate performance and capacity in production like conditions. It can show how these tests helped detect issues before they affected customers at scale.

title: Limited visibility of digital and cloud spend
description: Technology and cloud costs are seen as a single budget line. Teams have little insight into how costs relate to services, environments or customers. Surprises are common.

title: Basic cost reports for major platforms
description: Finance or platform teams produce periodic reports for key platforms or vendors. These may show spend by account or subscription. Mapping to services and teams is partial.

title: Service and team level cost views
description: Costs are allocated or tagged to services, environments or teams where feasible. Dashboards allow owners to see their spend over time. Large variances are investigated.

title: Cost visibility integrated into decision making
description: Cost information is used when prioritising work, selecting architectures and negotiating contracts. Teams can see the impact of changes on cost. Cost and resilience trade offs are surfaced.

title: Value oriented financial transparency
description: Cost views are combined with value metrics such as usage, revenue or mission outcomes. The organisation can explain which services are most expensive per unit of value and whether that is justified by resilience or other factors.

title: Reactive cost cutting
description: Cost reduction actions tend to be reactive, for example after a budget challenge. They may focus on headline items without considering risk or long term impact.

title: Simple optimisation of obvious waste
description: Teams close unused resources, reduce overprovisioning and cancel surplus licences when noticed. Some basic guidance exists on right sizing.

title: Structured optimisation program
description: There is a regular review of digital and cloud costs to identify optimisation opportunities. Actions such as right sizing, reserved instances or storage tiering are tracked. Savings targets are agreed with teams.

title: Optimisation aligned with resilience and performance
description: Cost efforts are balanced with resilience, security and performance needs. The organisation can show where it chose to spend more to reduce risk, and where it safely reduced spend. Technical and finance teams collaborate on decisions.

title: Continuous efficiency improvement
description: Efficiency is part of normal delivery and operations work. Teams monitor both cost and utilisation metrics. Savings from optimisation are reinvested in resilience, innovation or user experience.

title: High manual toil in operations
description: Many routine tasks such as log collection, user provisioning or environment setup are manual. Errors and delays are common. Automation opportunities are known but not prioritised.

title: Scripts and small automations in pockets
description: Individual engineers or teams write scripts and small tools to speed up recurring tasks. These are helpful but not documented or supported centrally.

title: Planned automation of key workflows
description: The organisation identifies high toil processes and prioritises them for automation. Workflow or orchestration tools are used for common tasks such as deployments, ticket routing or incident notification. Benefits are measured.

title: Automation as a shared platform capability
description: Platform teams provide reusable automation components, for example self service environments, standard pipelines or runbooks. Governance ensures automation is secure, reliable and maintained. Manual work in these areas reduces over time.

title: Automation optimised for resilience and people
description: Automation is designed to support resilient operations and reduce cognitive load, not just cost. The organisation can show where automation has prevented incidents or sped up recovery. Staff have time freed up for higher value work.

title: Unclear link between digital spend and value
description: Many systems persist due to history, not active choice. It is hard to say which services should be grown, maintained or retired. Value is assumed rather than measured.

title: Basic portfolio lists and priorities
description: There is a list of applications or services with rough criticality ratings. Decisions to invest or retire are made case by case, often driven by risk or vendor support dates.

title: Portfolio management with value and risk views
description: Services are grouped into a portfolio with information on cost, usage, risk and business owner. Periodic reviews decide where to invest, hold or retire. Some low value or redundant services are decommissioned.

title: Strategic alignment of digital portfolio
description: Portfolio decisions are clearly linked to strategy, resilience needs and customer outcomes. High value, high risk services receive priority investment. Low value, high cost services are targeted for redesign or retirement.

title: Dynamic portfolio shaped by outcomes
description: Portfolio decisions respond to changing conditions such as new channels, regulations or threats. The organisation can give examples where retiring or consolidating services reduced complexity and improved resilience and cost.

title: User experience and accessibility largely untested
description: Interfaces are designed based on developer or product intuition. Accessibility is rarely considered. Support relies on users calling or emailing when they struggle.

title: Basic UX and support for key services
description: Some user research or feedback informs design for important services. Support channels such as helpdesk or chat are available. Accessibility is considered in a limited way.

title: User centred design and support practices
description: Product teams use user research, usability testing and analytics for their services. Accessibility standards are applied to new developments. Support teams have knowledge bases and clear routes to escalate issues.

title: Integrated UX, resilience and support
description: User experience design explicitly considers errors, outages and degraded modes, for example clear messages and self service options. Support teams are involved in design and rollout. User feedback on reliability is monitored and fed into roadmaps.

title: Inclusive, resilient user experience
description: Services are designed to be accessible and usable for diverse users, including during incidents. The organisation can show how UX and support improvements have reduced user errors, support requests and operational load while improving resilience.

title: Operability considered late
description: Operational needs such as monitoring, runbooks and logging are added near go live if time allows. Operating a service can be complex and fragile.

title: Basic operability checklists
description: Some teams use checklists to ensure monitoring, alerts and access are in place before go live. Operators are briefed on new services but may lack deep understanding.

title: Operability requirements in design and build
description: Operability needs such as observability, configuration management, support tooling and access are captured during design. Operations staff or SREs review new services before launch. Issues found are fixed before acceptance.

title: Shared responsibility for operability
description: Product, engineering and operations share responsibility for keeping services healthy. Error budgets, operational reviews and support metrics influence planning. Operability improvements are planned and funded.

title: Operability by default
description: Design patterns and platforms make it easy to build operable services. The organisation can show that new services typically launch with strong operability and lower incident rates. Operability is part of the culture, not just a checklist.

title: Knowledge in people’s heads
description: Common tasks and incident responses rely on the memory of a few individuals. If they are unavailable, resolution is slow. Written instructions are rare or outdated.

title: Basic runbooks for some critical tasks
description: For some high impact incidents or maintenance tasks, there are simple runbooks or checklists. These may be stored in shared folders or wikis. Updates are ad hoc.

title: Structured runbooks and procedures
description: Common operational tasks and incident types have documented, step by step runbooks. Runbooks are referenced during incidents and training. Ownership and review cycles are defined.

title: Runbooks integrated with tooling
description: Runbooks are linked from monitoring and ticketing tools so responders can access them quickly. Some steps are automated or semi automated. Feedback from use is captured and used to improve content.

title: Living, tested operational knowledge base
description: Runbooks are regularly tested through drills or game days. Content evolves as systems and teams change. New staff can ramp up more quickly because procedures and context are clear and accessible.

title: Little focus on human factors in operations
description: On call, shift work and complex tooling create high cognitive load. Fatigue and stress are managed informally by individuals. Errors may be attributed to “human error” rather than system design.

title: Basic attention to shifts and workload
description: On call rotas and shift patterns exist, with some attention to fairness. Some guidance is given on taking breaks and handovers. Tooling may remain complex.

title: Consideration of human factors in design and process
description: Interfaces, alerts and procedures consider the people who use them. For example, alert floods are reduced, and handover templates are used. Leaders recognise burnout risks and act on feedback.

title: Proactive management of cognitive load and fatigue
description: Metrics such as alert volume, incident frequency and overtime are monitored. Capacity is adjusted to reduce chronic overload. Training and peer support are available for responders.

title: Human centred resilience practices
description: Human factors experts or trained staff contribute to incident reviews and design work. The organisation can show how changes to tooling, schedules or culture reduced human related errors and improved retention and performance.
